A man sold the Eiffel Tower,
and the buyer never called the police.
You see,
in 1925 the tower was rusting,
costly,
and Paris was openly talking about tearing it down.
So Victor Lustig printed fake government letterhead,
booked a fancy hotel suite,
and invited five scrap dealers to a secret meeting.
“The city can’t afford it,”
he whispered.
“Highest bid gets seven thousand tons of iron.
But tell no one, or there’ll be riots.”
One dealer, André Poisson, wanted it badly.
But something felt off.
So Lustig leaned in and confessed:
he was an underpaid official, and he’d need a little bribe.
That’s what sold it.
Because only a real official would ask for a bribe.
Poisson paid,
and Lustig was on a train
out of Paris with a suitcase of cash.
Then he waited for the police.
They never came.
Poisson was too embarrassed to admit he’d been fooled.
So a month later, Lustig came back…
and tried to sell it again.
